item.title: Thailand likely to employ 10,000 Bangladeshis
item.description:
Bangladesh and Thailand have discussed the prospect of employment for around 10,000 Bangladeshi workers in Thailand following completion of necessary procedures, alongside expanding bilateral cooperation in trade, investment and tourism.
The issue was discussed during a bilateral meeting between Prime Minister's Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir and Thai Deputy Foreign Minister Vijavat Isarabhakdi in Bangkok on Friday morning, according to a press release received here on Friday.
Humaiun held the meeting during a stopover in the Thai capital following his official visit to Manila, the Philippines.
During the talks, the two sides reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening the longstanding friendly relations between Bangladesh and Thailand and expanding cooperation in the areas of mutual interest.
They reviewed the overall state of bilateral relations and discussed ways to enhance cooperation in trade and investment, labour mobility, tourism and people-to-people contacts.
The two sides particularly exchanged views on the prospect of opening employment opportunities for around 10,000 Bangladeshi workers in Thailand once the necessary procedures are completed.
The Foreign Affairs adviser also sought Thailand's continued support for Bangladesh's inclusion as an Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partner.
In response, the Thai deputy foreign minister assured that Thailand would continue its constructive engagement on the matter.
Bangladesh has been seeking Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partner status as part of its broader efforts to deepen institutional engagement with the Southeast Asian regional bloc and strengthen economic and strategic ties with its member states.
During the meeting, Humaiun, on behalf of the prime minister of Bangladesh, also invited the Thai prime minister to visit Bangladesh at a mutually convenient time.

item.title: Info minister: All religious communities enjoy equal rights in Bangladesh
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon has said citizens of all religious faiths in Bangladesh enjoy equal rights, emphasizing that the country's constitution leaves no scope for discrimination or division based on religion.
"Sanatan believers enjoy the exact same rights as Muslims, Christians, and Buddhists in this country. Our constitution does not divide people on the basis of religion. Those who attempt to create division in the name of religion or politics are enemies of the nation, enemies of religion, and enemies of the Almighty," he said.
The minister made the remarks while addressing as the chief guest at a discussion organized on the occasion of Sri Sri Jagannathdev's Ulto Rath Yatra at the Dhakeshwari National Temple in the capital on Friday.
Swapon highlighted that the Sanatan faith represents a thousand-year-old heritage and history bears witness to its long-standing continuity.
"Throughout human civilization, spiritual leaders across all faiths are striving to reach the Almighty. True believers respect and revere followers of other faiths because everyone is ultimately seeking the same Supreme Power, regardless of the ritual or path they follow," he added.
The minister urged everyone to stay vigilant against forces attempting to exploit religious sentiments for narrow political gains or societal division, both domestically and regionally.
"Staying firm in one's own faith while showing deep respect to other faiths to ensure peaceful coexistence is the true essence of a non-communal and inclusive society," Swapon stressed.
He further underscored that under the philosophy of Bangladeshi nationalism—as outlined by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman—no division based on religion, caste, language, or geography will be tolerated.
Inaugurating the event, Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) Administrator Abdus Salam stated that Bangladesh belongs equally to all communities.
"Those who seek to undermine communal harmony do not truly believe in Bangladesh's sovereignty. People of the Hindu faith fought alongside us during our Liberation War, and this nation was achieved through shared sacrifices. There is no scope for anyone to be considered a second-class citizen here; every citizen shares equal rights," Salam noted. Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad President Basudeb Dhar also spoke on the occasion as special guest.

item.title: Khalilur: Bangladesh to work closely for stronger Asean
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman has reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to working closely with Asean and its partners to strengthen regional cooperation in tackling emerging and transnational threats.
Addressing the commemorative ceremony marking the 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC) in Manila, he stressed the need for practical and coordinated initiatives to bolster global resilience against pandemics, climate shocks, cyber incidents and supply chain disruptions, said a foreign ministry press release here on Friday.
Dr Khalilur said joint early-warning systems, shared risk assessments and regional crisis-response mechanisms could play an important role in strengthening collective preparedness and resilience against such challenges.
The foreign minister also outlined ways to address emerging threats posed by AI-enabled cybercrime as well as misinformation and disinformation spread through social media.
The TAC, signed five decades ago, establishes principles governing relations among states in the region, including mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity and non-interference in internal affairs.
Bangladesh acceded to the TAC in 2007, becoming one of the first South Asian countries to formalize a treaty-based commitment to Asean’s normative framework.
On the sidelines of the TAC anniversary events, Dr Khalilur Rahman also held separate bilateral meetings with the foreign ministers of Chile, the Netherlands and the Philippines, as well as Qatar’s state minister for Foreign Affairs.
The meetings covered a range of issues of mutual interest, including trade and investment, energy supply, water-resource management, legal migration and the circular economy.
Khalilur Rahman is currently visiting Manila to attend the 33rd Asean Regional Forum (ARF) Foreign Ministers’ Meeting and commemorative activities marking the 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia.

item.title: Dhaka among 10 districts at risk as monsoon intensifies
item.description:
Bangladesh is bracing for another spell of stormy weather as an active southwest monsoon intensifies over the country, prompting the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) to issue warnings of thunderstorms, gusty winds and heavy rainfall across large parts of the country.
On Friday, the BMD forecast temporary gusty or squally winds of 45-60km/h, accompanied by rain or thunderstorms, over Dhaka, Faridpur, Khulna, Barisal, Patuakhali, Noakhali, Comilla, Chittagong, Cox's Bazar and Sylhet. Inland river ports in these districts have been advised to hoist Local Cautionary Signal No. 1.
The latest warning comes amid an increasingly active southwest monsoon, which has already triggered intermittent rain in several regions over the past week and is expected to continue influencing weather conditions in the coming days.
For the capital, the BMD forecasts partly cloudy to cloudy skies with rain or thundershowers throughout the day. South to southeasterly winds are expected to blow at 10-15km/h, while daytime temperatures are likely to remain nearly unchanged.
Official observations showed Dhaka recorded a temperature of 25.2°C at 6am on Friday, with 98% relative humidity, reflecting highly moisture-laden conditions. The city received 8mm of rainfall during the previous 24 hours, while Thursday's maximum temperature reached 31.2°C.
Meteorologists said the combination of high humidity and recurring rainfall is likely to keep conditions uncomfortable despite slightly lower temperatures.
According to the BMD's 24-hour nationwide forecast, most places in Dhaka, Khulna, Barisal and Chittagong divisions, along with many areas of Rajshahi, Rangpur, Mymensingh and Sylhet divisions, are likely to experience light to moderate rain or thundershowers accompanied by temporary gusty winds.
The department also warned of heavy to very heavy rainfall in Khulna, Barisal and Chittagong divisions, raising the risk of urban flooding, waterlogging and localized flash floods.
In the Chittagong Hill Tracts and adjoining hilly areas, prolonged rainfall may further increase the risk of landslides.
Meteorologists attribute the current weather pattern to an active southwest monsoon drawing abundant moisture from the Bay of Bengal. Combined with local atmospheric instability, the system is creating favourable conditions for widespread cloud formation, thunderstorms and intense rainfall.
Bangladesh typically experiences short-duration but high-intensity downpours during the monsoon season, particularly in coastal and southeastern districts.
Meteorologist Dr Md Bazlur Rashid said rainfall activity is expected to remain above normal over the next several days.
"The monsoon is currently active over Bangladesh, and this is likely to sustain widespread rain and thunderstorms across many parts of the country," he said.
He added: "Heavy to very heavy rainfall remains possible, particularly in the southern and coastal districts. People using waterways and those staying in open areas should closely follow official weather advisories."
Experts warned that the impacts of the current weather system extend beyond heavy rainfall.
High-intensity downpours could overwhelm urban drainage systems, worsening waterlogging in Dhaka, Chattogram and other major cities. Low-lying areas may experience temporary flooding, while prolonged rainfall in hilly regions could heighten the risk of landslides.
Lightning also remains one of Bangladesh's deadliest monsoon hazards. Authorities have advised people to avoid open fields, rivers, tall trees and electrical poles during thunderstorms, while operators of small boats have been urged to suspend operations when cautionary signals are in force.
With the monsoon expected to remain active through the weekend, the BMD said it will continue issuing updated forecasts and warnings as conditions evolve, urging residents to remain vigilant and follow official weather advisories.

item.title: Can Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections calm tensions?
item.description:
The first phase of local elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir is scheduled for Monday, July 27, amid calls for a boycott from the recently outlawed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (Jaac), a grassroots alliance of civil society groups.
The Jaac has been demanding the abolition of 12 seats in the regional assembly reserved for people displaced from India-administered Kashmir and living in Pakistan. It argues that only residents of Pakistan-administered Kashmir should be eligible to contest regional elections.
The dispute escalated after the Supreme Court of Pakistan-administered Kashmir ruled that the refugee seats are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.
The regional government outlawed the Jaac in June under anti-terrorism laws, citing threats to public order, and detained dozens of its supporters.
The ban came amid rising tensions over the refugee seats and ahead of violent protests sparked by the group’s campaign to scrap them.
The unrest has left around 30 people dead since June, according to local estimates cited by Reuters news agency.
India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir in its entirety, but each country only controls a section of the territory, making the Muslim-majority region a longstanding flashpoint between the nuclear-armed neighbors since their independence from Britain in 1947.
Since early June, Pakistan-administered Kashmir — known locally as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) — has witnessed weeks of protests and sit-ins. While the dispute over the refugee seats has become a major flashpoint, Jaac has also campaigned for broader economic and governance reforms.
Following the unrest, authorities split polling into three phases, with voting in Mirpur set for July 27 and elections in the protest-hit Poonch division postponed until August 10.
Voting in the regional capital Muzaffarabad has been delayed until August 2 over security concerns. The Jaac continues to stage a sit-in in Rawalakot, near the Line of Control with India.
As the region heads to the polls, a major question is whether the elections can restore public confidence or merely offer a temporary pause in public anger.
“We are just asking for fair representation, which is our right,” Ali Raza, a 22-year-old student protester in Rawalakot told DW. “The local people who live here should have the right to choose their representatives, not the refugees who settled here from India.”
“The election is a major opportunity for the people of AJK to choose their representatives,” said Shazia Marri, the central information secretary of the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP), which currently rules the region. “The people want their rights protected, their issues addressed, and a government that delivers on its promises.”
However, Jaac leaders argue that elections alone cannot resolve the issues that brought thousands of people onto the streets.
“Our movement is not replacing one government with another over time; we need our rights, but there are just political slogans in the campaigns,” one Jaac official told DW under condition of anonymity.
Imran Khan, a geopolitical expert and former director of the US Institute of Peace Pakistan, expects the movement to continue post-elections.
“While elections in AJK are important on their own merit and for the continuity of the political process, they will not address the political grievances and demands of the people who are supporting Jaac,” Khan told DW. “The protest is outside the assembly. They no longer trust those institutions fully.”
Analysts say the Jaac protests marked a significant shift in Pakistan-administered Kashmir’s politics by bringing together citizens across party lines around economic and governance issues rather than traditional political rivalries.
For analyst Khan, Jaac is a dominant political force to reckon with in quite significant parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.
“They have more street credibility than mainstream politicians and parties despite the allegations of foreign backing and funding. For now, they have disrupted the status quo politics in AJK,” Khan said, noting that the Pakistani establishment has the means and methods to break up such political movements.
Experts caution that rebuilding trust will require more than campaign promises.
“[The] next government in AJK will be very weak, as it will be sandwiched between pressure from both the Pakistani establishment that controls AJK through administrative and security framework and the sentiment on the street, which is very pro Jaac,” argued Khan.
He added that the next government would have “little credibility and limited room to govern unless it reaches an understanding with Jaac to ease political tensions.”
But politician Marri believes that trust is rebuilt by listening to people’s concerns, delivering practical solutions, and empowering elected institutions.
If key grievances remain unresolved, analysts warn that another wave of protests cannot be ruled out.
“It is too early to say that more waves of protests will be seen, but Jaac has the potential to become a lasting political force,” said Khan, who suggested the group risks being weakened by internal divisions and pressure from the establishment.
“For now, both sides are treading carefully, with Jaac relying on mass support and the establishment avoiding a full crackdown while buying time,” Khan added.
While the vote will determine who governs Pakistan-administered Kashmir, it is unlikely to resolve the broader constitutional dispute over Kashmir or eliminate long-standing frustrations with the region’s governance.
“Governments must listen to public concerns and address them through dialogue and effective governance. Stability comes from listening to people, respecting the law, and delivering results,” Marri added.
For Raza, the Gen Z protester, “The world has changed, and we have seen governments toppling through student protests in the neighboring countries; we won’t stop, and protests will continue until our rights have not been given to us.”

item.title: Klopp handed task of reviving Germany's football fortunes
item.description:
Jurgen Klopp was named as the new head coach of the German men's national football team on Friday, replacing Julian Nagelsmann who left after the team's disappointing World Cup.
"We're very happy to be able to present Jurgen Klopp today as the new coach," German Football Association (DFB) President Bernd Neuendorf told a press conference in Frankfurt.
Neuendorf said Klopp's contract would run until "summer 2030, so until the next World Cup in Morocco, Spain and Portugal," adding that the contract would begin on August 15.
Klopp, 59, had spoken publicly of his desire to take on the role after Nagelsmann left earlier in July.
Germany crashed out of this summer's World Cup after losing to Paraguay on penalties in the round of 32.
It was the third successive World Cup failure for the Germans since winning their fourth title in 2014.
Germany failed to make it past the group stage in both 2018 and 2022. They have won just one knockout match at the past five major tournaments, reaching the quarter-finals as hosts at Euro 2024.
Klopp had successful coaching tenures at German clubs Mainz -- where he was a player for more than a decade -- and Borussia Dortmund before turning round the fortunes of English giants Liverpool.

item.title: NCP demands arrest of Mohammed Shahabuddin following resignation as president
item.description:
The National Citizen Party (NCP) has demanded the arrest of Mohammed Shahabuddin following his resignation from the office of President.

The party voiced this demand during a press briefing held on Friday evening at its central office in Banglamotor, Dhaka.

NCP Member Secretary Akhter Hossen stated that Shahabuddin must be arrested immediately to ensure complete justice for the sacrifices of the martyrs of the 2024 mass uprising and to prevent the resurgence of an autocratic system.

He added that if the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) truly upholds the spirit of the July Mass Uprising, it should swiftly initiate legal action against the former president.

Akhter Hossen alleged that the resigned president was an accomplice to fascism who legitimised all forms of enforced disappearances and killings under former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.

Furthermore, during the 2024 uprising, when Sheikh Hasina perpetrated atrocities against students and the public, Shahabuddin tacitly endorsed her actions through his silence, the NCP senior leader added.

Akhter also remarked that although Shahabuddin stepped down citing ill health, he incorporated irrelevant historical narratives into his resignation letter in what was essentially an attempt to construct a 'safe exit' for himself.

Criticising the BNP in this context, member of parliament Akhter Hossen noted that the BNP had been informed long ago that Shahabuddin was unfit to hold the presidency. However, rather than impeaching him at the time, the BNP helped consolidate his position by involving him in various social and state functions.

The NCP leader asserted that while immunity had previously shielded Shahabuddin from legal proceedings due to his office, his resignation leaves him with no remaining legal protection.

Speaking at the briefing, NCP Senior Joint Convenor Ariful Islam Adeeb stated that the BNP wishes to install its own nominee in the presidency during the upcoming election period, which is why it initiated moves to remove the president five months after forming the government.

He added that the BNP has a history of placing pliable individuals in the presidency to secure electoral advantages, and that the current political maneuvering is merely a continuation of this longstanding strategy.

Also present at the briefing were NCP member of parliament Abdul Hannan Masud and NCP leader Monira Sharmin, among others.

item.title: Japan to test rare-earth mining 6 km underwater
item.description:
JAPAN-CHINA-MINING-OCEANS-CLIMATE

Japan said Friday it plans to conduct full-scale mining tests in February for rare earth minerals from a seabed near a remote Pacific island, after a mission successfully recovered samples from six kilometres below the waves.

Japan and the United States, as well as many other countries, are seeking to curb dependence on China for the valuable minerals used in an array of high-tech products from missiles to wind turbines.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said that the samples taken earlier this year by a deep-sea drilling ship from a depth of around 6,000 metres (about 20,000 feet) near Minami Torishima included traces of yttrium.

Yttrium "is globally scarce and is used in coating agents for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, catalysts for purifying harmful nitrogen oxides in exhaust gases, and in the semiconductor and automotive industries, making it an important rare earth for our country", Takaichi said on X.

"Based on this achievement, we plan to conduct a full-scale mining test in February next year."

Japan will "undertake efforts to strengthen the supply chain resilience, with the full involvement of both government and private sectors, so as not to overly depend on specific countries", Takaichi added.

The Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC) said separately that gadolinium and dysprosium, two other rare-earth elements, were also detected in the 50 tonnes of seabed material recovered.

In March, Takaichi said that she would discuss cooperation with the United States on mining around the coral atoll, which is some 2,000 kilometres (1,250 miles) from Tokyo and also known as Minamitorishima.

Previous studies have suggested that the surrounding seabed could contain millions of tonnes of rare earths which might ensure supplies of some minerals for many hundreds of years.

Environmental campaigners warn deep-sea mining threatens marine ecosystems.

China accounts for almost two-thirds of rare earth mining production and 92 percent of global refined output, according to the International Energy Agency.

A spat with Beijing sparked by comments by Takaichi about Taiwan in November has seen China heavily restrict supplies to Japan.

Officials said in March that they also planned to conduct a preliminary survey on Minami Torishima, uninhabited by civilians and off-limits to tourists, as a possible site for nuclear waste.

item.title: Bomb recovered beneath Motijheel metro station
item.description:
Police have recovered an improvised explosive device (IED) concealed inside an umbrella beneath the Motijheel metro rail station in the capital.

The device was subsequently rendered safe by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) bomb disposal unit.

According to DMP sources, the device was found on the road beneath the Motijheel metro station at around 7:30 pm on Friday. The suspicious package, hidden inside an umbrella, caused panic among passers-by.

On information, police members quickly cordoned off the area before the DMP’s bomb disposal and disposal team arrived at the spot and successfully neutralised the device. Traffic on the affected road was temporarily suspended during the operation.

Niaz Mehdi, Additional Deputy Commissioner of the DMP’s Media and Public Relations Division, told Prothom Alo that the recovered device was an improvised explosive device (IED).

He said it had been safely removed and rendered inoperative. Police and other law enforcement agencies are now working to identify those responsible for placing the device inside the umbrella.

Witnesses said a loud explosion was heard while the bomb disposal team was carrying out the controlled detonation to neutralise the device.

Contacted for comment, MRT Police Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Siddiqi Tanzilur Rahman told Prothom Alo that he was occupied preparing an official report and was therefore unable to speak about the incident.

However, an officer on duty at the MRT Police Control Room confirmed that the device had been recovered from the roadside beneath the metro station. As a result, traffic movement on the adjacent road was temporarily halted, although Metro Rail services continued to operate normally throughout the incident.

Opposition says Shahabuddin must face trial, not just resign
item.description:
Opposition party leaders on Friday said president Mohammed Shahabuddin's resignation was not enough, insisting he should now face legal action over his alleged role during and after the deadly 2024 crackdown on the anti-Sheikh Hasina uprising.
Shahabuddin, 76, submitted his resignation letter on Friday afternoon, citing Autonomic Neuropathy, a condition that has reportedly caused episodes of temporary loss of consciousness.
Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad accepted the resignation at 5:01pm.
His departure comes nearly two years before the end of his five-year term, following months of pressure from opposition parties and student leaders. It also comes amid reports that he remained in contact with former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who is living in exile in India and has said she intends to return to Bangladesh around December.
Under the Constitution, the Speaker of the National parliament will discharge the president's duties until a new head of state is elected within 90 days.
NCP: Resignation should have been impeachment, not an exit route
National Citizen Party (NCP) Member Secretary Akhter Hossain said Shahabuddin should have been removed through impeachment rather than allowed to resign.
He alleged that the president tacitly supported the killings during the 2024 crackdown by failing to intervene and by empowering those responsible.
Hossain also cited Shahabuddin's controversial remarks after Hasina's ouster—including his statement that he had not seen her resignation letter—and what he described as a series of unconstitutional actions during his presidency.
Now that Shahabuddin no longer enjoys presidential immunity, Hossain said there is no legal barrier to prosecuting him. He called for a fair trial, saying accountability was essential to erase what he described as a "stain" on the nation.
The NCP, formed by student leaders of the 2024 uprising, has long campaigned for Shahabuddin's removal, accusing him of acting as a collaborator of the ousted Awami League government. The party contested the recent general election as part of an alliance led by Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami.
Jamaat: He failed as the nation's constitutional guardian
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman said Shahabuddin had failed in his constitutional duty as the guardian of the state.
He alleged that the president never condemned the killings during the crackdown, never called for an end to the violence, and never described the actions as unjust or oppressive. According to Shafiqul, Shahabuddin's silence amounted to tacit support for the crackdown.
Background
Shahabuddin had served as Bangladesh's largely ceremonial president since April 2023, overseeing one of the country's most turbulent political periods, including the aftermath of Sheikh Hasina's ouster during the student-led uprising in 2024.
A UN report said nearly 1,400 people were killed in the crackdown on the uprising. Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal later sentenced Hasina to death in absentia over the violence, a verdict she has rejected while in exile.
Following Hasina's removal from power, Shahabuddin came under sustained pressure from student groups that spearheaded the uprising, which accused him of siding with the former regime and demanded both his resignation and arrest.
Reuters reported on Thursday that Shahabuddin's resignation was imminent, days after Hasina announced plans to return to Bangladesh and surrender following her conviction.
The government led by Tarique Rahman took office in February after winning a landslide victory in the general election, ending 18 months of interim administration under Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus. Shahabuddin's departure leaves Awami League without an ally in the country's highest constitutional office ahead of Hasina's planned return.

item.title: Tuku: Take toughest possible measures against drugs to protect youth
item.description:
State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin Tuku on Friday called for the toughest possible measures against drugs, urging everyone to remain vigilant from their respective positions to protect the younger generation and help build a prosperous nation.
He made the remarks while addressing a function as the chief guest at Sonar Bangla Community Centre in Tangail.
On the occasion, he distributed scholarships, crests and certificates among around 500 meritorious students from playgroup to Class 10 of schools and madrasahs under an initiative of Tangail unit of Teachers Foundation Central Committee.
Presided over by Dr Khandakar Anisul Haque, the function was also addressed by Tangail district BNP President Md Hasanuzzamil Shaheen, former Member Secretary of Tangail district BNP Mahmudul Haque Sanu and Instructor of UPTC, Ajmiriganj, Habiganj, Md. Islam Mia, as the special guests.
Tuku said everyone has a responsibility to remain vigilant from their respective positions to prevent the spread of narcotics and guide the younger generation in the right direction.
He said nation-building is a shared responsibility and emphasized that protecting young people from drug abuse is essential for developing skilled, moral and patriotic citizens.
The state minister said Prime Minister has already introduced the "Notun Kuri" competition so that students can develop themselves as skilled and competent individuals by participating not only in academic studies but also in co-curricular activities.
Tuku said today's meritorious students would lead the way in building a prosperous Bangladesh in the future. Therefore, families, teachers and society must work together to nurture their talents, he added.
He said students should not only excel in examinations but also grow into ideal citizens enriched with morality, human values and patriotism.
General Secretary of Teachers Foundation Central Committee, Tangail, Mamunur Rashid, Literary Affairs Secretary Babu Bhobesh Mukut Pal, along with teachers, students, guardians and distinguished guests, were present at the programme.

item.title: BGB foils push-in attempt at Kushtia, Chapainawabganj borders
item.description:
Members of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) on Friday thwarted an alleged attempt by India's Border Security Force (BSF) to push eight people into Bangladesh through Daulatpur border in Kushtia.
According to BGB, the incident occurred around 5:10 am near border pillar 152/1-S under the Jaipur Border Outpost (BOP) in the Mahishkundi area of Pragpur union.
The paramilitary force said members of the 146 BSF Battalion's Char Meghna camp tried to force eight unidentified people into Bangladesh by making them cross a river. The group comprised two men, four women and two transgender persons.
After noticing the matter, a BGB patrol team immediately took position along the border and prevented them from entering Bangladesh, the force said. The group was later forced to return to the Indian side through the river, foiling the alleged push-in attempt.
Lieutenant Colonel Rashed Kamal Rony, commanding officer of Kushtia Battalion (47 BGB), said the force remains vigilant to prevent illegal infiltration and any attempt to violate border laws.
He said BGB is carrying out its duties with professionalism, vigilance and responsibility to ensure border security and maintain peace and order in border areas.
In Chapainawabganj, BGB foiled an alleged attempt by India's Border Security Force (BSF) to push seven individuals into Bangladesh through the Charaldanga border in Gomostapur upazila.
Lieutenant Colonel Mohammad Ariful Islam Masum, commanding officer of Naogaon Battalion (16 BGB), said members of the 12 BSF Battalion's Tilashan Camp allegedly tried to push the seven men into Bangladesh around 6:30am through the border near pillar 219/24-R/2.
He said a BGB patrol team detected the attempt and prevented the men from entering Bangladesh.
They are currently staying on the Indian side of the zero line along the border, Masum said, adding that the paramilitary force is closely monitoring the situation to prevent any further push-in attempts.

item.title: Land minister: Government gives highest priority to health, education sectors
item.description:
Land Minister Mizanur Rahman Minu on Friday said the government has attached the highest priority to the health and education sectors and will continue extending all-out support for the development of healthcare services across the country.
He made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at the closing ceremony of a three-day congenital heart disease screening and treatment programme for children aged between three and 18 at the Rajshahi National Heart Foundation.
The programme, held from July 22 to 24, was jointly organised by the Rajshahi National Heart Foundation, the Department of Pediatric Cardiology of China's Fuwai Yunnan Cardiovascular Hospital, and the National Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases and Hospital (NICVD), Dhaka.
Highlighting Bangladesh-China relations, the minister said the historic friendship between the two countries was initiated by Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman and has reached a new height following Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's recent visit to China.
Referring to infrastructure development, Minu announced that a special project would be undertaken to widen the road linking the Court-Natore Road with the Rajshahi National Heart Foundation.
He directed the Rajshahi City Corporation and the Rajshahi Development Authority (RDA) to take the necessary steps to implement the project. He also assured that the Ministry of Health would provide a special grant for the second-phase development of the Rajshahi National Heart Foundation.
The minister stressed the need to ensure world-class healthcare facilities in Rajshahi by utilizing China's advanced medical technology and expertise.
The function was chaired by Rajshahi National Heart Foundation President Md. Abdul Mannan.
Among others, Deputy Director-in-Charge of China's Fuwai Yunnan Cardiovascular Hospital and leader of the Chinese expert team Lu Jiang, Divisional Commissioner Dr ANM Bazlur Rashid, Rajshahi Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mohammad Faizul Kabir, Deputy Commissioner Kazi Shahidul Islam, NICVD Department Head and National Heart Foundation Life Member Prof. Dr. Md. Ataul Haque, National Heart Foundation Hospital and Research Institute Chief Consultant and Director Prof. Dr. Md. Rais Uddin, and National Heart Foundation Vice Presidents Hasen Ali and Maksudul Karim Samrat addressed the programme.

item.title: Bomb-like objects recovered beneath Motijheel Metro Rail Station
item.description:
Police recovered several bomb-like objects from beneath the Motijheel Metro Rail Station in the capital and safely defused them on Friday.
The matter was confirmed at around 8:30pm by Abdul Salam, investigation officer of Motijheel Police Station.
According to police, the bomb disposal unit of the Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) division of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) defused 2 suspicious objects. The area was cordoned off while members of law enforcement agencies collected evidence from the scene.
Abdul Salam said police received information shortly after 7pm that bomb-like objects had been placed beneath the Motijheel Metro Rail Station. Officers from the local police station and the CTTC bomb disposal unit then rushed to the scene.
He said: “So far, 2 bomb-like objects have been rendered safe.”
According to sources familiar with the development, the recovered objects appeared to be improvised explosive devices (IEDs) fitted with circuits and batteries.
The sources said each device contained approximately 1-1.5kg of sulfur packed inside a pipe, commonly known as a pipe bomb, along with numerous small iron balls intended to act as shrapnel. They also claimed the device could have detonated if a button concealed in an umbrella had been pressed.

item.title: Commerce minister: Govt to set up health centers in tea garden areas
item.description:
Commerce, Industries, Jute and Textiles Minister Khandaker Abdul Muktadir on friday said the government will soon establish healthcare centers in tea garden areas across the country to improve access to primary medical services for underserved communities.
Speaking as the chief guest at the inauguration of a daylong free medical camp for tea workers at Sylhet Government High School in Sadar Upazila of Sylhet, the minister said the health sector remains one of the government's highest priorities.
He said the government plans to gradually increase public expenditure on both the health and education sectors to 5% of GDP in the coming years. Highlighting the government's recent initiatives, Muktadir said several measures have already been undertaken to strengthen healthcare services in Sylhet.
"The establishment of a 250-bed hospital has already been approved and is currently under process. In addition, health centers will soon be set up in tea garden areas so that residents can access basic healthcare without having to travel to the city," he added.
Responding to questions about the United States' tariff policy, the minister said the US had reinstated an existing tariff under a new designation after the expiration of the previously announced 150-day period.
"This is essentially a replacement of the previous tariff rather than the imposition of a new duty. Therefore, there has been no effective change in the tariff situation," he said.
On fuel prices, Muktadir said the government continues to subsidize petroleum products despite fluctuations in the international market and has no plans now to raise fuel prices.
The event was chaired by Sylhet Deputy Commissioner Abdul Al Mamun and conducted by Sylhet Sadar Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Khoshnur Rubaiyat.
Among those present as special guests were Sylhet City Corporation Administrator Abdul Qayyum Chowdhury, Sylhet-6 MP Advocate Emran Ahmed Chowdhury, Sylhet Development Authority Chairman Rezaul Hasan Qayes Lodi, Sylhet District Council Administrator Abul Kaher Chowdhury Shamim, Sunamganj District Council Administrator Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury, and Sylhet Medical University Vice-Chancellor Dr. Ziaur Rahman Chowdhury.
The daylong medical camp attracted a large number of tea garden workers and local residents from across Sylhet, providing free general healthcare, eye treatment, maternal and child health services, and family planning consultations.

item.title: Fakhrul vows democratic reforms, economic recovery
item.description:
Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Friday said the government is committed to restoring democratic institutions, rebuilding the economy and implementing the commitments outlined in the July National Charter.
"Democracy is under pressure across the world, and Bangladesh is no exception. Our responsibility is to practise democracy, nurture democratic values and build a liberal, non-communal and humane society," he said.
Speaking at the inaugural session of a two-day Bengal Delta Conference-2026 organised by the Dacca Institute of Research and Analytics (DAIRA) at a city hotel, Fakhrul paid tributes to the martyrs of the 1971 War of Liberation and those who lost their lives during the 2024 student-led mass uprising, describing their sacrifices as the foundation for a democratic and inclusive Bangladesh.
"I salute the young people who made history through their movement and made it possible to remove fascism," he said, remembering those who sacrificed their lives for democracy.
Describing himself as "a political activist" rather than an academic, Fakhrul, also BNP secretary general, said his experience in movements against dictatorship and authoritarianism shaped his belief in democratic governance.
He said Bangladesh is passing through a critical period marked by economic and political challenges, aggravated by global conflicts, including the Russia-Ukraine war and tensions in the Middle East, as well as the impacts of economic mismanagement and money laundering.
"We are fighting for a comeback," the minister said, adding that the government inherited a difficult economic situation characterised by unemployment, weak investment and a fragile banking sector.
He said the current government is working to restore economic stability while rebuilding democratic institutions, noting that political parties had reached broad consensus on constitutional reforms through the July Charter, aimed at creating a more stable and development-oriented political framework.
"Our leader Tarique Rahman is committed to implementing the July Charter, and we are equally committed to fulfilling the promises made to the people through our election manifesto," Fakhrul said.
Highlighting the government's priorities, he said programmes such as Family Card, Farmers’ Card, social safety allowances, support for religious leaders, canal excavation projects and incentives for agriculture are beginning to generate positive economic impacts.
The BNP leader also said the latest national budget reduced taxes and tariffs in several sectors to encourage industrial growth, while giving greater emphasis to agriculture and the creative economy by integrating ethnic communities and local innovators into mainstream economic development.
On political reforms, he said a parliamentary committee has already been formed to work on constitutional amendments, reaffirming the government's commitment to strengthening democratic institutions.
The Bengal Delta Conference under the theme "Bangladesh and a Changing World: Uncharted Times, Emerging Orders, and the Politics of Care" brings together scholars, policymakers, diplomats, civil society representatives and young researchers to discuss governance, the economy, regional affairs and Bangladesh's evolving role in a rapidly changing global order.

item.title: Benapole Customs sets revenue target of Tk 10,588cr despite Tk 4,731cr shortfall
item.description:
The National Board of Revenue (NBR) has set a revenue collection target of Tk 10,588 crore for Benapole Customs House in the 2026–27 fiscal year, despite a Tk 4,731 crore revenue shortfall from the previous fiscal year. The new target is Tk 702 crore lower than the revised target set for FY 2025–26.
According to customs sources, the revised revenue target for FY 2025–26 was Tk 11,290 crore, but Benapole Customs collected only Tk 6,559 crore by the end of the fiscal year, leaving a deficit of Tk 4,731 crore. During the same period, imports through Benapole Port also declined by nearly 197,000 metric tons.
Officials said the revised target for the current fiscal year has been set at a more realistic level in view of the significant revenue shortfall and the decline in import volumes.
Customs officials remain optimistic about achieving the new target. However, business leaders argue that the goal will be difficult to meet unless legal imports are expanded, customs clearance is expedited, unnecessary trade restrictions are removed, and smuggling and revenue evasion are brought under strict control.
Customs sources also revealed that more than 100 cases of fraud have been detected at Benapole Customs over the past six months. In addition, four cases filed last month over the alleged smuggling of goods worth nearly Tk 20 crore have named 57 individuals as accused. Investigations and legal proceedings are currently underway.
Ziaur Rahman, General Secretary of the Benapole Importers and Exporters Association, said that achieving the revenue target would require an increase in import activities as well as greater transparency in trade. He stressed the need for stricter measures to curb smuggling, under-invoicing, and other irregularities.
Rahat Hossain, Assistant Commissioner of Benapole Customs House, said customs officials are working diligently to enhance revenue collection. He added that disciplinary action against those involved in irregularities and the recovery of fines are continuing, while all necessary initiatives are being taken to achieve the revenue target for the current fiscal year.

item.title: Phone line, security in place as Shahabuddin prepares to leave
item.description:
A new telephone line is being installed at the Gulshan residence where outgoing President Mohammed Shahabuddin is expected to move after leaving Bangabhaban.
On Friday afternoon, employees of the Bangladesh Telecommunications Company Limited (BTCL) arrived to install the connection.
According to security guards at the building, Shahabuddin is expected to reside on the fifth floor after stepping down. They said he visited the residence 3 to 4 days ago, accompanied by more than 100 people, including members of law enforcement agencies.
Sources said minor renovation and other preparation work at the residence has already been completed. Several members of the Special Branch (SB) are also stationed there.
Abdur Razzak, a Telecommunications Mechanic (TCM) at Bangladesh Telecommunications Company Limited (BTCL), said the installation was being carried out following official instructions. He said: “We have officially been sent here to install a new telephone line. The previous line was disconnected after he became President. Therefore, we are now installing a new one.”
President Mohammed Shahabuddin resigned from office, and his resignation letter was accepted by Speaker of the National Parliament Hafiz Uddin Ahmed. The letter was submitted to the speaker on Friday.
In the resignation letter, Shahabuddin said he was stepping down due to serious illness.

item.title: Former presidents who left office before completing their terms
item.description:
Bangladesh’s 22nd President Mohammed Shahabuddin resigned on Friday, citing serious health complications, becoming the latest head of state to leave office before completing his constitutional term. His resignation letter was submitted to Speaker Hafizuddin Ahmed on Friday afternoon.
Since independence, Bangladesh’s presidency has been shaped by assassinations, military coups, constitutional changes, mass uprisings, and political crises. Of the 18 individuals who have served as president in a full, acting, or in-charge capacity, 10 left office before completing their terms.
Shahabuddin joins a list of presidents who resigned, were removed from office, lost power through military coups, or left because of political disagreements, mass protests, or health complications. Two sitting presidents were assassinated, while only one died of natural causes in office.
Justice Abu Sayeed Chowdhury, Bangladesh’s 3rd president, assumed office on January 12, 1972, after Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman became prime minister under the parliamentary system.
He resigned on December 24, 1973, before completing his tenure, reportedly following disagreements with the government on several issues. Mohammad Mohammadullah subsequently assumed the presidency.
Mohammad Mohammadullah first assumed the presidency in an acting capacity on December 24, 1973, following the resignation of Justice Abu Sayeed Chowdhury. He was sworn in as the country's fourth president on January 27, 1974.
His tenure ended on January 25, 1975, when Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman returned to the presidency after Bangladesh adopted a presidential system under the Fourth Amendment and the formation of BAKSAL.
Khondaker Mostaq Ahmad assumed power following the assassination of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and most members of his family on August 15, 1975. He declared himself president and led the government for 81 days.
During the Liberation War, Mostaq served as minister for foreign affairs, law, and parliamentary affairs in the Mujibnagar government. After independence, he held several cabinet portfolios under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and later became a member of the executive committee of BAKSAL.
His presidency ended on November 6, 1975, when he was removed from power in a military coup.
Chief Justice Abu Sadat Mohammad Sayem became Bangladesh’s president on November 6, 1975, after Khondaker Mostaq Ahmad stepped down. He formally assumed office on November 8 and became the country’s first civilian president under martial law.
Sayem simultaneously served as Chief Martial Law Administrator (CMLA) before relinquishing that role on November 29, 1976.
He resigned as president on April 21, 1977, citing deteriorating health.
Following the assassination of President Ziaur Rahman in May 1981, Vice President Abdus Sattar became acting president before winning the presidential election on November 15, 1981, securing around 66% of the vote. The election, however, remained controversial.
His presidency ended on March 24, 1982, when Army Chief Hussain Muhammad Ershad staged a military coup. At the time, Sattar declared that he was unable to continue performing presidential duties because of ill health, effectively relinquishing office.
General Hussain Muhammad Ershad assumed the presidency on December 11, 1983, after removing President Ahsanuddin Chowdhury from office.
During his rule, Bangladesh held general elections in 1986 and 1988, both of which drew criticism over their credibility.
As opposition to military rule intensified, major political parties united in a nationwide movement demanding Ershad’s resignation. He resigned on December 6, 1990, following the mass uprising, ending nearly 9 years of military-backed rule.
AQM Badruddoza Chowdhury assumed office as Bangladesh’s 15th president on November 14, 2001, but resigned on June 21, 2002, after around 7 months in office amid mounting pressure from the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP).
Party lawmakers reportedly threatened to impeach him over several issues, including his decision not to pay tribute at former president Ziaur Rahman’s grave on his death anniversary and not referring to Zia as the “proclaimer of independence” in an official message. His visit to Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s mausoleum was also reported to have contributed to the party’s dissatisfaction.
Bangladesh’s political history has also witnessed the deaths of sitting presidents while in office.
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the country’s first president, was assassinated along with most members of his family in a military coup on August 15, 1975, while serving as president.
President and Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) founder Ziaur Rahman was assassinated during a military coup in Chittagong on May 30, 1981.
President Zillur Rahman remains the only Bangladeshi president to have died of natural causes while in office. Bangladesh’s 19th president died on March 20, 2013, while undergoing treatment at Mount Elizabeth Hospital in Singapore.
Mohammed Shahabuddin’s resignation adds another chapter to the history of Bangladesh’s presidency, an office that has frequently been shaped by political upheaval, military intervention, institutional tensions, and health-related departures.

item.title: From Pudong to Dhaka: Tale of two cities
item.description:
Over a decade before South Asia gained its first underwater expressway—the Karnaphuli Tunnel in our port city of Chittagong—I experienced under-river travel for the very first time during a road trip from Puxi to Pudong in China.
In the early winter of 2012, I left Puxi, the historic urban core of Shanghai on the west bank of the Huangpu River. Crossing the tunnel beneath the water, I landed on the Lujiazui peninsula.
Lujiazui, the prominent financial and commercial district on the eastern bank, immediately greeted me with its strikingly high skyline. I kept looking up, neck bent and chin raised, as the skyscrapers of the Pudong New Area left me awestruck.
Up until then, I had never seen such a dense concentration of tall buildings in a single city. I quickly realized that Pudong was a massive, sprawling district, and Lujiazui was just its crowning jewel—a hyper-modern neighborhood housing the financial hub.
Even after all these years, I vividly remember the sheer scale of the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Dressed in dark sunglasses, a green button-down shirt, and a dark blazer, I stepped onto the trading floor, where millions of Yuan worth of shares must have already changed hands that day. The entrance to this bustling bourse featured large glass-panel facades, heavy structural pillars, revolving doors, and stepped granite stairs where visitors and professionals constantly passed through.
The writer standing in the Lujiazui financial district of Pudong, standing between landmark skyscrapers – 1,380 feet Jin Mao Tower and 1,614 feet Shanghai World Financial Center. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Stepping back out onto the streets from one of the world’s busiest financial hubs, the architecture continued to command my attention. At one point, I stood directly between two of China's most iconic supertall skyscrapers.
On one side rose the 88-story Jin Mao Tower, featuring a traditional Chinese pagoda-inspired tiered design that tapers gently to 1,380 feet. On the other stood an even taller, sleek, dark-blue glass giant—the 1,614-foot Shanghai World Financial Center, famously nicknamed "The Bottle Opener" due to the large trapezoidal aperture at its peak designed to reduce wind pressure.
Reflecting on Shanghai's incredible urban development, I eventually stopped at the base of the iconic Oriental Pearl Tower. Famous for its futuristic design featuring 11 spheres of varying sizes, the 1,535-foot structure was the tallest in China from its completion in 1994 until 2007. Hungry by this point, I caught the fast-moving elevator to dine at the revolving restaurant inside the tower's lower pink-and-silver sphere.
After a delicious lunch and a great dining experience, I walked out onto the famous glass-bottom skywalk of the observation deck. Standing on the outdoor transparent glass module 850 feet in the air, I looked directly down at the plaza and streets below.
From this vantage point, the distinctive pointed roof of the Bank of Shanghai Headquarters and the surrounding skyscrapers were sharply visible, while the Huangpu River snaked through the landscape far below. Before leaving, I also caught a fascinating sneak peek of the Shanghai History Museum situated directly underground.
Remarkably, about five years after witnessing these urban marvels, I had a rare chance to meet one of the masterminds behind Shanghai’s transformation. What made it even more special was that the meeting took place in my own hometown—Dhaka.
In 2017, the World Bank brought Professor Zhu Ruolin, a renowned urban planner and former dean of the Pudong Planning and Design Institute, to Bangladesh. The goal was to leverage his expertise for the future expansion and new town development of Dhaka, which has become one of the world’s most populous, congested, and underserved cities.
Professor Zhu Ruolin. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Professor Zhu had been an instrumental figure in the master planning, architectural zoning, and urban development of Pudong, transforming it from a patchwork of paddy fields and farmland in the early 1990s into a global financial hub. Under his leadership at the institute, Shanghai expanded eastward across the Huangpu River, eventually emerging as the world's most populous city.
The writer along with a local host standing in front of the primary entrance plaza of the Oriental Pearl Tower in Shanghai, China. Behind them the distinctive large red greeting wall features the gold lettering “欢迎您” (Huānyíng nín) – Welcome. Located in the Pudong New Area of Shanghai, Oriental Pearl TV Tower stands right at the tip of the Lujiazui peninsula, the prominent financial district on the eastern bank of the Huangpu River. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
It was deeply rewarding to speak with this visionary man, who expressed confidence that Dhaka, too, could be transformed into a highly developed city. He explained that Pudong—China's answer to Manhattan—now boasts one of the world's leading stock exchanges, a major international airport, and a futuristic skyline because of an intentional multi-billion-dollar facelift that began during China's economic opening in the 1980s.
Visitors posing together outside the Jin Mao Tower plaza area in the Lujiazui financial district of Pudong, Shanghai. The tall totem sign in the center background reads J·LIFE, a high-end retail, dining, and lifestyle center located inside the podium of the Jin Mao Tower. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
In 1990, leaders in Beijing unveiled plans to develop the area east of the river into a Special Economic Zone, and three years later, the "Pudong New Area" was officially born.
Zhu then told me: “In 1992, Pudong was an underdeveloped area. In order to develop the area, we welcomed foreign investment and interest there.” He had said the authority invited five designers to submit their ideas to transform Pudong into a modern city. “We didn't accept or reject any submission. We prepared a fresh design taking all the good points from all five.”
Ever since my visit to Pudong in 2012 and my meeting with Professor Zhu in 2017, I have found myself wondering: how long will it take for us to see a successfully planned urban expansion in Purbachal? Why is it so difficult to transform Dhaka the way they transformed Shanghai?
Professor Zhu's words still echo in my ears today. He emphasized that everything they achieved in Pudong was driven by visionary thinking, well-thought-out plans, effective management, and coordinated efforts.
“A city is like a human body," he told me. "If you don't take care of it, she will get sick.”
Looking at the state of our capital today, I cannot help but ask: isn't Dhaka sick enough yet?
The main entrance to the Shanghai Stock Exchange Building, located in Pudong, Shanghai, China. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune

item.title: New president likely from BNP Standing Committee
item.description:
Discussion has intensified in the political arena over the election of the country’s next president following the resignation of President Md. Shahabuddin. After Shahabuddin stepped down at 5:00pm on Friday, attention has now turned to who will become the next president.

Although the names of several senior BNP leaders had been discussed for the post since the formation of the government, a few new names have been added to the list of potential candidates over the past two days. However, according to reliable sources, the shortlist has now become much more limited.

A source who plays an important role in policymaking for both the government and the BNP told Prothom Alo on Friday that the country’s next president may come not from outside the party but from among the members of the BNP’s highest policymaking body—the National Standing Committee.

President Shahabuddin resigns, Speaker to assume presidential duties

However, the matter has not yet been discussed at any party forum. The source said preparations are underway at the BNP’s top level to choose the successor to outgoing President Md Shahabuddin, with considerable caution.

Since the BNP formed the government on 17 February, the names of several party leaders have been discussed as possible candidates for the presidency. Among them are senior leader Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain and Secretary General Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir.

The names of Standing Committee members Abdul Moyeen Khan and Nazrul Islam Khan have also been discussed. More recently, Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Ghani has been added to the list of names under consideration. The name of a former chief justice has also surfaced in discussions.

Multiple responsible sources within and outside the BNP said several senior party leaders have fallen behind in the race for the presidency due to health issues and other considerations. Over the past two days, discussions have increasingly centred on the name of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam.

Amid growing speculation over new faces for the presidency, a section within the party has become active in promoting Mirza Fakhrul Islam as the next president.

At the same time, many of Mirza Fakhrul Islam’s well-wishers outside politics also consider him a suitable candidate for the presidency. Some have expressed this view on social media. Professor Asif Nazrul, former law adviser to the interim government led by Professor Muhammad Yunus, described Mirza Fakhrul Islam as the “best candidate” for the presidency.

In a Facebook post titled “Who Will Be the Next President of Bangladesh?” on Friday, he wrote: “In my opinion, Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir is the most suitable person for this position. During Sheikh Hasina’s authoritarian rule, he led the party as secretary general, endured persecution in many ways and made significant sacrifices. Among politicians, he is one of the most moderate, courteous and eloquent.”

According to Professor Asif Nazrul, “There are a few other suitable people in the BNP. However, in my opinion, considering all aspects, Mirza Fakhrul would be ahead. If a politician is to be made president, he is probably the best candidate.”

Earlier, BRAC Bangladesh Executive Director Asif Saleh also explained in a Facebook post why Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir would be a more suitable choice for the presidency than others.

Following Md Shahabuddin’s resignation on Friday, Speaker of the National Parliament Hafiz Uddin Ahmed assumed the responsibilities of the president in accordance with the Constitution. He will continue to serve in this role until a new president is elected.

According to Article 123 of the Constitution, if the office of the president falls vacant due to resignation, death or removal, a new president must be elected within 90 days. The president is elected by members of parliament.

As the BNP holds a majority in parliament, the party’s nominated candidate is expected to be elected. Over the past several days, the identity of the next president has been a major topic of discussion among BNP leaders and activists as well as in wider political circles.

The discussion is expected to continue until a new president is elected or the party formally announces its decision.

However, a senior official at the Prime Minister’s Office said there is still time before the presidential election is held. Given political realities, the situation can change quickly.
